whatItDoes: Estimates the home price you can afford based on your annual income, other monthly debts, available down payment, mortgage rate, and the maximum debt-to-income ratio you choose to allow.
whyItExists: Lenders approve based on the debt-to-income ratio, but approvals don't tell you what keeps your budget comfortable. This calculator back-calculates a realistic price from your own affordability rule.
whoShouldUse: First-time buyers setting a price range, families checking budget limits, and anyone comparing how a larger down payment changes affordability.
useCases: Set a realistic home price range before shopping
See how other debts shrink your budget
Test how a higher down payment expands your range
Check if your dream price fits your DTI cap
instructions: Enter your annual household gross income
Enter other monthly debt payments (cards, auto, student loans)
Enter the down payment you have available
Set a mortgage rate, term, and the max DTI you want
Read the affordable home price and monthly housing budget
examples: $90,000 income, $40,000 down, 6.5% for 30 years at 36% DTI -> affordable approx $290,000
$120,000 income, $60,000 down, 6% for 30 years at 36% DTI -> affordable approx $430,000
bestPractices: Keep a buffer — use 36% DTI even if a lender allows 43%
Include a realistic mortgage rate, not a teaser
Remember property tax, insurance, and HOA are not in the number
Re-run after any income, rate, or down payment change
commonMistakes: Entering net instead of gross income
Forgetting other debts like car and student loans
Using the maximum approval without a comfort buffer
Ignoring taxes, insurance, and HOA in the real payment
faq: What is a good DTI to use? — 36% is a common comfortable cap; lenders may stretch to 43%.
Does this include property taxes? — No, those are added on top of the mortgage.
Can I lower the payment by increasing down payment? — Yes, try a larger down payment and re-run.
Is my data shared? — No, everything runs locally in your browser.
